■AI業界が提示する安全性の論点
・9月12日、アモデイCEOはエッセイを通じてAI開発のペース調整を訴えた。これは技術的な能力向上が社会実装に追いつかないという懸念から来ている。

record.text: How to identify Shadow AI traffic: the signals we've found actually useful

external.description: How to identify Shadow AI traffic: the signals we've found actually useful Shadow AI detection sounds simple until you actually try to build it. At first, the obvious approach is: Maintain a list of ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Perplexity, etc. -> detect traffic -> classify it as AI. But that breaks down surprisingly quickly. Take GitHub as an example. An employee visiting GitHub is not necessarily using Shadow AI. The same employee using GitHub Copilot potentially is. The same problem exists with Gmail/Gemini, Microsoft 365/Copilot, Slack AI, Notion AI, IDE extensions, browser extensions, and hundreds of SaaS products embedding AI into otherwise legitimate applications. So the real problem is not: "Is this domain an AI domain?" It is: "Does this particular interaction involve a user sending data to an AI system?" We have been working on this problem while building Shadow AI detection at Walled AI, and these are some of the signals I have found most useful. 1. Known AI domains and endpoints This is the easiest layer. Maintain intelligence for known:AI domainsinference endpointsAPI pathsmodel providersAI-specific subdomainsSaaS AI endpoints For something like `api.openai.com`, confidence is obviously high. But domain-level detection becomes much weaker when AI functionality is embedded inside a larger application. So domain intelligence should be the first signal, not the final classifier. 2. Request characteristics The request itself can provide surprisingly useful signals. For example:POST requestsrelatively large text payloadsJSON structures containing message- or prompt-like fieldsconversation historymodel identifiersgeneration parametersdocument or image uploads associated with an inference request None of these individually means "AI." A large POST request could simply be someone submitting a form. But several of these appearing together can increase confidence considerably. 3. Response characteristics The response can provide another independent signal. LLM applications often exhibit patterns such as:streamed responsesServer-Sent Eventstoken- or chunk-style incremental outputlong generated-text responsesa request followed by sustained incremental response traffic Again, streaming does not automatically mean AI. Plenty of legitimate applications stream data. But: prompt-like request + AI-looking endpoint + streamed generated response is substantially stronger than any one of those signals alone. 4. Browser context matters This becomes particularly useful for embedded AI. The browser often knows more than the network does. It can potentially tell you:which page the employee is onwhat UI element initiated the interactionwhether a prompt box existswhether text or files are being submittedwhether the employee switched into an AI featurewhether the user is on a personal or enterprise AI account This helps distinguish: GitHub -> normal development activity from: GitHub -> Copilot interaction without simply classifying all GitHub traffic as AI. This is one reason I do not think Shadow AI discovery can ultimately be solved through network intelligence alone. We have documented some of the multi-layer detection architecture we are building here: Shadow AI Detection: Discover, Monitor & Control Unauthorized AI | WalledAI5. Identity is another signal Finding an AI service is not necessarily enough. Consider: ChatGPT Enterprise -> approved versus Personal ChatGPT account -> unapproved The destination may effectively be the same while the governance implications are very different. Ideally, AI detection should therefore be correlated with:userdevicedepartmentaccount or tenantapplicationapproved or unapproved status At that point, you are moving beyond traffic classification into actual Shadow AI discovery. 6. Use confidence scoring instead of binary rules This is probably the biggest architectural lesson. Instead of: IF domain == X -> AI I would rather think about: Domain signal + endpoint signal + request signal + response signal + browser signal + identity signal -> AI confidence score High-confidence traffic can be classified deterministically. Low-confidence traffic can remain unclassified. The interesting part is the middle.7. Use an LLM classifier only for ambiguous traffic One tempting solution is to send everything to an AI classifier. Technically, that is possible. Economically and operationally, it is probably not what you want. If you are inspecting endpoint traffic at enterprise scale, pushing every ambiguous HTTP interaction through an LLM adds:costlatencycompute requirementsanother potential privacy considerationanother dependency in the enforcement path We have therefore been experimenting with a different philosophy: Rules and patterns first -> confidence scoring -> LLM judge as fallback As the deterministic detection library improves, fewer requests should require expensive classification. In other words, the system should ideally become **cheaper and faster as its detection intelligence improves**. 8. Detection is only half the problem Once you have classified something as AI traffic, you can start answering more useful governance questions: Which AI applications are employees using? Which are approved versus unapproved? Which departments are adopting Shadow AI? Is sensitive information being submitted? Which models and services are receiving organizational data? What was allowed, redacted, or blocked? This is where we are feeding discovery and enforcement telemetry into the Walled AI Governance Dashboard, so security teams can get a consolidated view of AI usage rather than a large collection of individual network events: AI Governance Dashboard: Audit Logs & Alerts | WalledAIReal-time AI usage monitoring, audit logs, policy-violation alerts and board-ready compliance reports across ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot and internal LLMs.walled.ai Walled AIA practical architecture Known intelligence -> Network signals -> Request + response patterns -> Browser context -> Identity -> Confidence scoring -> LLM fallback rather than: List of AI domains -> Block The hardest part is not identifying ChatGPT. It is identifying AI functionality embedded inside otherwise legitimate applications without creating an unacceptable number of false positives. Curious how others working on Shadow AI are approaching this. What signals have you found reliable for distinguishing actual AI interactions from normal application traffic?
